title: [2504.07274] Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities

sections.heading: Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities

content.text: ♠\spadesuit

Recent advances in language modeling have led to growing interest in applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to financial problems, enabling new approaches to analysis and decision-making. To systematically examine this trend, we review 374 NLP research papers published between 2017 and 2024 across 38 conferences and workshops, with a focused analysis of 221 papers that directly address finance-related tasks. We evaluate these papers across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions, identifying key trends such as the increasing use of general-purpose language models, steady progress in sentiment analysis and information extraction, and emerging efforts around explainability and privacy-preserving methods. We also discuss the use of evaluation metrics, highlighting the importance of domain-specific ones to complement standard machine learning metrics. Our findings emphasize the need for more accessible, adaptive datasets and highlight the significance of incorporating financial crisis periods to strengthen model robustness under real-world conditions. This survey provides a structured overview of NLP research applied to finance and offers practical insights for researchers and practitioners working at this intersection.

Language modeling has become a key tool in natural language processing (NLP) for analyzing unstructured text, including reports, news articles, and social media posts. These methods are increasingly applied to finance-related tasks such as sentiment analysis ([Balakrishnan et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib9)), information extraction ([Huang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib37)), summarization ([Khanna et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib49)), stock prediction ([Jain & Agrawal 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib44)), and volatility forecasting ([Niu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib79)). Given the increasing number of NLP papers addressing financial problems, there is a need to systematically examine how the field is contributing to finance-related applications. While prior surveys have examined this intersection (Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), many adopt a qualitative approach ([Chen et al. 2022b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib16); [Gao et al. 2021b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib32); [Xiao et al. 2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib108)), focusing on broad NLP techniques ([Jagdale & Deshmukh 2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib43); [Man et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib70); [Liu 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib64)), deep learning ([Ozbayoglu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib80)) and Large Language Models (LLMs) ([Nie et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib78); [Li et al. 2023c](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib58)), or specific tasks such as sentiment analysis ([Mishev et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib75)). However, these studies often lack systematic evaluation.

In this study, we focus specifically on NLP research applied to finance. Our scope includes papers published in NLP venues where methods are developed, benchmarked, or adapted for financial problems. We analyze 374 papers published from 2017 to 2024 across 38 NLP conferences and workshops. After further filtering (Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2 "2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), we retain 221 papers that directly address finance-related tasks. These are evaluated across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions, including tasks, methodologies, datasets, evaluation metrics, and accessibility.

Our analysis reveals several patterns in the current research landscape. Commonly addressed tasks include sentiment analysis, information extraction, and question answering, while areas such as explainability and privacy-preserving techniques are explored less frequently (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Standard machine learning metrics are widely used for evaluation, although these may not always reflect domain-specific priorities (Section [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Most studies focus on stable market conditions, with less attention to more volatile periods (Section [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and relying on outdated sources or overlooking issues such as survivorship bias (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) Finally, we observe a trend toward the use of general-purpose language models over custom architecture (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While this reflects the rapid integration of recent advances in NLP, further exploration of domain-specific strategies may offer additional value for finance-related tasks.

To study how NLP has been applied to finance, we selected papers from 38 NLP venues, including CoLM, ACL, NAACL, EMNLP, LREC, COLING, and workshops like FinNLP and the Workshop on Economics and Natural Language Processing. The full list of venues is provided in Table [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5 "Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). As illustrated in Figure [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), we began by filtering papers that mentioned “finance” or “financial” in their abstracts. Out of all such papers published from 1975 to the present, more than 94% were published from 2017 onward. This growth coincides with the emergence of transformer-based models ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib103)), which greatly expanded the scope of NLP applications. Accordingly, we use 2017 as a threshold year for our analysis.

| Category | Description | | --- | --- | | Financial Forecast (Category I) | Targets predicting financial events, including stock movements, volatility, bankruptcy, and currency exchange rates. | | Financial Resources (Category II) | Covers tasks addressing finance-specific issues beyond prediction, such as constructing financial datasets, detecting fraud in finance-related documents, and extracting financial events. | | Financial Applications (Category III) | Focuses on general ML/NLP tasks like sentiment analysis and information/relation extraction for financial datasets. | | Finance Related (Category IV) | Covers tasks not applied to financial data or targeting financial problems, but potentially useful in finance, such privacy-preserving and explainable AI. |

This initial filtering returned 374 papers. Among them, 88 were tied to shared tasks (e.g., SemEval-2017 ([Kar et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib48)), FinCausal-2022 ([Mondal et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib76))), and 65 used the term “financial” in a different contexts – such as referencing financial resources ([Sekeres et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib90); [Ding & Riloff 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib23)) – without any actual financial application. After removing these, we retained 221 papers for our analysis.

Unlike previous surveys, which often emphasize qualitative observations, our study combines both qualitative and quantitative methods to provide a broader view of the field. We categorized the selected papers by their primary focus, resulting in four task-based categories (Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). This classification helps us examine trends in how NLP techniques are being used to tackle finance-relevant problems and supports more detailed comparisons across types of tasks.

children.heading: 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications

content.text: To understand how NLP has been used in financial contexts, we categorized papers into four groups (shown in Table [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) based on their primary tasks (Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). This classification helps map how language modeling techniques are applied and how directly each paper engages with finance, with Category I representing the most direct financial use cases. Detailed descriptions of each category are provided in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A4 "Appendix D Task Description ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities").

Financial Forecast (Category I) papers cover predictive tasks such as stock price and volatility forecasting. While these areas are well-studied, others like economic forecasting ([Arno et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib8)), risk assessment ([Zhou et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib124)), and cryptocurrency prediction ([Seroyizhko et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib91)) receive less focus. These areas present opportunities for expanding the reach of prediction models and improving their robustness and comparability (Section [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7 "7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

Financial Resources (Category II) papers often focus on dataset construction (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). These datasets – ranging from annotated earnings calls to news and speeches – support tasks like financial event extraction ([Huang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib38); [Ju et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib47)), fraud detection ([Erben & Waldis 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib28); [Wang et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib105)), and annotation ([Aguda et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib4); [Khatuya et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib50)). Although these tasks contribute to enhancing financial data processing, other tasks remain relatively underrepresented.

In the Financial Applications (Category III) group, sentiment analysis ([Rodriguez Inserte et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib83)), information extraction ([Lior et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib60)), and question answering ([Kosireddy et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib53)) are the dominant tasks. These methods are widely used to analyze earnings calls, reports, and market commentary, where investor sentiment and factual extraction are key inputs for decision-making. Recent efforts have aimed to improve QA models for handling financial text ([Theuma & Shareghi 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib98); [Liu et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib63); [Mavi et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib72)).

Finally, among Finance-Related (Category IV) papers, the most studied areas are dataset construction and numerical reasoning. While these datasets are not finance-specific, they have potential applications in finance. For instance, fake news detection datasets ([Vargas et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib102)) can help reduce misinformation in markets. Numerical reasoning ([Akhtar et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib6)), important for understanding financial statements and assessing risk, is receiving more attention. However, other areas – such as explainable AI (XAI) ([Klein & Walther 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib52)) and privacy-preserving methods ([Abbe et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib1)) – remain rarely explored, despite their relevance to secure and interpretable decision-making ([Basu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib10)).

Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Language Models) shows how quickly language models are adopted for finance-related NLP tasks. While early models like BERT ([Devlin et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib22)) took 13 months to appear in these applications, recent models – GPT-3.5, GPT-4 ([Achiam et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib2)), and Mistral ([Jiang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib45)) – were adopted within 6–12 months. LLaMA-2 ([Touvron et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib99))) saw integration in just 5 months, reflecting the community’s increasing speed in applying general NLP advances to financial tasks.

As shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Language Models), general-purpose models – LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, and Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) like BERT and RoBERTa ([Liu et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib65))) – are used far more frequently than domain-adapted ones. BERT appears in over 70 papers, while finance-tuned models such as FinBERT ([Araci 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib7); [Yang et al. 2020b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib116); [Liu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib66); [Huang et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib36)), FinMA ([Xie et al. 2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib110)), and FinGPT ([Yang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib114)) are less common. Notably, earlier FinBERT versions are more widely used than later ones, suggesting that improvements in general models often outweigh the benefits of domain-specific adaptation.

Custom models were common before 2022, especially for tasks like table-based QA (e.g., TagOp for TAT-QA ([Zhu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib125)), HyBrider for HybridQA ([Chen et al. 2020c](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib18))). Some models, like MDRM ([Qin & Yang 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib82)), HTML ([Yang et al. 2020a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib115)), and HAN ([Hu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib35)), are still used as baselines, particularly in volatility prediction ([Niu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib79); [Mathur et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib71)). However, the rise of general LLMs has led to a sharp decline in custom architectures. As a result of the accelerated development and deployment of these general purpose models, researchers increasingly rely on adapting pretrained models instead of building domain-specific ones from scratch.

The OL and FD sections of Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") highlights the scarcity of non-English datasets for forecasting tasks such as return or volatility prediction. One exception is CMIN ([Luo et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib67)), which includes English and Chinese financial data. Most datasets use English-only sources like EDGAR filings ([Maheshwari et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib69)) and financial news ([Xie et al. 2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib111)), which may limit model performance in non-English markets. Creating multilingual forecasting datasets would support broader applicability and reduce language bias, as also noted by [Jørgensen et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib46).

Since 2017, research applying NLP to finance has shifted from custom models toward general-purpose pretrained architectures. New models are adopted faster than before, and general PLMs have largely replaced finance-specific ones. This preference also influences dataset use: most forecasting datasets are English-only, limiting generalization to global markets.

children.heading: 5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance

content.text: To understand the methodological landscape, we grouped the approaches used in the surveyed papers into nine categories (Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A3 "Appendix C Common Methods used ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Common Methods used ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While the total number of papers has grown, methods like statistical NLP, conventional machine learning, and embeddings have remained mostly flat. In contrast, there has been a sharp increase in the use of deep learning, PLMs and LLMs, reflecting the field’s shift toward pretrained architectures.

As seen in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), the first three categories – statistical NLP, embeddings, and conventional ML – have persisted but have seen reduced usage as PLMs and LLMs take lead. The rise began with models like BERT in 2019, which significantly improved context handling in financial texts ([Li et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib55); [Chen et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib17); [Ein-Dor et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib27)). PLMs are now widely used for tasks such as summarization and entity recognition. Since 2023, LLMs like ChatGPT-3.5 have seen rapid adoption ([Tang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib97); [Li et al. 2023a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib56); [Ni et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib77)), especially for text generation ([Guo et al. 2023b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib34)) and financial QA ([Uluoglakci & Temizel 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib100)). This transition has also brought more complex deep learning architectures used for multi-step reasoning and domain-specific challenges ([Ma et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib68); [Zhao et al. 2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib120); [Su et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib95)).

While pretrained models dominate, several methods remain underused despite their promise. Statistical modeling, graph-based approaches, and knowledge graphs could improve model robustness and interpretability, particularly for applications like causality detection ([Tabari et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib96)) or market dynamics ([Menzio et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib73)). Emerging techniques like GraphRAG ([Edge et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib26)) highlight the potential of such methods, yet they appear in only a fraction of papers. Their limited presence suggests opportunities for expanding methodological diversity in future research.

As the adoption of language models accelerates, the issue of open accessibility in NLP research, especially in finance, becomes more relevant. As shown in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6 Code & Data Accessibility ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), open-source practices have become more common in recent years. Before 2021, closed-source code dominated, but the trend has shifted toward sharing code and datasets. This move enhances transparency, reproducibility, and collaborative progress in NLP research applied to finance ([Whited 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib106)). Despite this, some papers still include inactive links or empty repositories, limiting reproducibility. At the same time, dataset availability has steadily increased since 2017, pointing to growing awareness around open data. Maintaining functional, up-to-date repositories remains essential to support meaningful benchmarking and model development.

Category I papers reveal several areas where forecasting models could be improved. Most studies use general ML metrics, leaving out finance-specific measures that better capture practical utility. Crisis periods are rarely considered, limiting insights into how models behave under stress. Finally, there is a strong U.S. and English-language bias in data, with limited adoption of global financial datasets. Expanding these areas of exploration could strengthen model robustness and support broader real-world applicability.

As shown in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Category I papers mostly rely on ML metrics like accuracy, F1, or MSE ([Sawhney et al. 2020b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib87); [Wu 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib107); [Yangjia et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib117)). While useful, these do not fully reflect financial performance. Only three financial metrics appear more than once – Sharpe Ratio, Maximum Drawdown, and Cumulative Return (defined in Appendix [G](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A7 "Appendix G Glossary ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

Finance-specific metrics offer risk-adjusted insights that ML measures overlook. Sharpe Ratio, for example, evaluates return relative to risk ([Zou et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib127)). Incorporating such metrics would improve comparability across models and align research outcomes with practical needs ([Zhang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib118); [Zou et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib127); [Sawhney et al. 2021b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib89)).

Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") shows that data usage begins to rise after 1993, when electronic filings became publicly available, with another increase in 2005 following the HTML filing mandate ([U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib101)). However, usage dips around 2009 and 2020 – years associated with the global financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic. These periods are essential for evaluating model robustness, yet they remain underused, likely due to data availability challenges prior to 2015 ([Bloomberg L.P. 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib11)).

Despite these constraints, crisis periods offer valuable testing grounds. Most models are trained on stable conditions, which may not reflect their behavior during volatility. Including data from crises enables stress testing ([Investopedia Staff 2025b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib42)) and helps build forecasting models that remain reliable under instability.

children.heading: Commonly Used and Overlooked Data Sources

content.text: Most forecasting models use common financial sources: stock prices, SEC filings, financial news, earnings calls (e.g., MDRM ([Qin & Yang 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib82)), StockNet ([Xu & Cohen 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib113))). But many valuable datasets are either rarely used (e.g., Federal Reserve reports ([Menzio et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib73))) or completely absent from NLP research. Public resources like FRED ([Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib30)) and Fama-French ([Fama & French 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib29)) offer rich macroeconomic indicators that remain unexplored. Incorporating these datasets could help capture macroeconomic trends and market dynamics, improving model reliability.

Access limitations are also a concern. Legacy datasets like MDRM are outdated, and APIs such as Yahoo Finance’s have been discontinued. Others, like CRSP, require paid access. This limits reproducibility and restricts access to reliable, up-to-date data. There’s a clear need for open, regularly updated datasets applicable for financial forecasting.

This paper presents a systematic, quantitative analysis of NLP research applied to finance. From an initial pool of 374 papers across major NLP venues (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5 "Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), we curated a final set of 221 papers after filtering. We categorized them by primary task (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and assessed each across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions (Table [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix B Various Dimensions surveyed ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S8.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 8 Discussion & Conclusion ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") summarizes key trends and identifies opportunities where language modeling research can further contribute to finance-related problems.

| Criteria | Trends and Observations | Potential Opportunities and Recommendations | | --- | --- | --- | | NLP Tasks in Finance | Sentiment analysis, information extraction, and question answering are the most frequently addressed tasks. Forecasting is mostly centered around stock and volatility prediction. | Underexplored areas such as explainability, privacy-preserving methods, and tasks like bankruptcy or cryptocurrency prediction present valuable directions for future work (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | PLM/LLM Adoption | General-purpose PLMs and LLMs have largely replaced finance-specific and custom architectures. At the same time, the use of statistical NLP and conventional ML continues to decline (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | Revisiting finance-specific models and exploring alternative methods such as graph-based learning or hybrid statistical models could offer improvements for financial tasks (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S5 "5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | Evaluation Metrics | Most studies rely on ML metrics such as accuracy and MSE, which do not reflect financial performance. | Incorporating financial metrics like Sharpe Ratio or Maximum Drawdown would improve the practical relevance and comparability of predictive models (Section [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | Crisis Periods | Few studies include data from financial crises such as 2008–2009 or 2020–2021, focusing instead on stable periods. | Including data from volatile periods can support stress-testing and help build models more resilient to real-world fluctuations (Section [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | Data Selection and Bias | Most studies use English-language datasets and U.S.-based financial sources. While there is growing diversity in the types of data used (e.g., news, filings, social media), much of it is static, with limited updates or adaptation to changing financial contexts. | Developing multilingual and globally representative datasets, along with maintaining and updating existing ones, would support better generalization and long-term applicability of models across financial domains (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | Open Accessibility | Code and dataset sharing has become more common, especially after 2021, enhancing transparency and reproducibility. | Open access should be a standard in NLP-for-finance research when legally feasible. Maintaining functional and up-to-date repositories is key for long-term reproducibility (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6 Code & Data Accessibility ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). |

NLP research applied to finance has largely centered on a few core tasks – sentiment analysis, information extraction, and question answering – while underexploring others like explainability and privacy-preserving methods (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). The rapid adoption of PLMs and LLMs has made it easier to apply language models, but has also led to reduced methodological variety (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Graph-based models, statistical techniques, and other alternatives remain underused despite their potential (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S5 "5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While open-source practices have become more common, researchers should be more careful about maintaining functional and up-to-date repositories to ensure long-term reproducibility and meaningful benchmarking (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6 Code & Data Accessibility ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). In addition, adopting financial-domain metrics can make evaluations more meaningful and aligned with practical goals (Section [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Including crisis periods in datasets (Section [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and improving data selection practices (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) can help ensure robustness and consistency. More diverse datasets, especially beyond English and U.S. markets, are also needed to broaden applicability (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

While NLP methods are increasingly used in financial contexts, several challenges remain. Many models are trained on static or incomplete datasets, leading to biases that may affect predictions (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Evaluations often omit real-world considerations such as market volatility and financial risk (Sections [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Incorporating financial benchmarks and testing models under stress conditions could improve their practical value. Continued progress in this direction can better align research outcomes with decision-making needs in financial settings.

This study does not assess the merit or quality of individual papers. We do not suggest that any category or method is inherently better than others. Our goal is to map the volume and distribution of research applying NLP methods to finance, and to offer a foundation for further study, without making judgments about the value of specific approaches.

###### Abstract

Recent advances in language modeling have led to growing interest in applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to financial problems, enabling new approaches to analysis and decision-making. To systematically examine this trend, we review 374 NLP research papers published between 2017 and 2024 across 38 conferences and workshops, with a focused analysis of 221 papers that directly address finance-related tasks. We evaluate these papers across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions, identifying key trends such as the increasing use of general-purpose language models, steady progress in sentiment analysis and information extraction, and emerging efforts around explainability and privacy-preserving methods. We also discuss the use of evaluation metrics, highlighting the importance of domain-specific ones to complement standard machine learning metrics. Our findings emphasize the need for more accessible, adaptive datasets and highlight the significance of incorporating financial crisis periods to strengthen model robustness under real-world conditions. This survey provides a structured overview of NLP research applied to finance and offers practical insights for researchers and practitioners working at this intersection.

chunks.text:
## 1 Introduction

Language modeling has become a key tool in natural language processing (NLP) for analyzing unstructured text, including reports, news articles, and social media posts. These methods are increasingly applied to finance-related tasks such as sentiment analysis ([Balakrishnan et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib9)), information extraction ([Huang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib37)), summarization ([Khanna et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib49)), stock prediction ([Jain & Agrawal 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib44)), and volatility forecasting ([Niu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib79)). Given the increasing number of NLP papers addressing financial problems, there is a need to systematically examine how the field is contributing to finance-related applications. While prior surveys have examined this intersection (Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), many adopt a qualitative approach ([Chen et al. 2022b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib16); [Gao et al. 2021b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib32); [Xiao et al. 2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib108)), focusing on broad NLP techniques ([Jagdale & Deshmukh 2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib43); [Man et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib70); [Liu 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib64)), deep learning ([Ozbayoglu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib80)) and Large Language Models (LLMs) ([Nie et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib78); [Li et al. 2023c](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib58)), or specific tasks such as sentiment analysis ([Mishev et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib75)). However, these studies often lack systematic evaluation.

In this study, we focus specifically on NLP research applied to finance. Our scope includes papers published in NLP venues where methods are developed, benchmarked, or adapted for financial problems. We analyze 374 papers published from 2017 to 2024 across 38 NLP conferences and workshops. After further filtering (Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2 "2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), we retain 221 papers that directly address finance-related tasks. These are evaluated across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions, including tasks, methodologies, datasets, evaluation metrics, and accessibility.

Our analysis reveals several patterns in the current research landscape. Commonly addressed tasks include sentiment analysis, information extraction, and question answering, while areas such as explainability and privacy-preserving techniques are explored less frequently (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Standard machine learning metrics are widely used for evaluation, although these may not always reflect domain-specific priorities (Section [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Most studies focus on stable market conditions, with less attention to more volatile periods (Section [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and relying on outdated sources or overlooking issues such as survivorship bias (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) Finally, we observe a trend toward the use of general-purpose language models over custom architecture (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While this reflects the rapid integration of recent advances in NLP, further exploration of domain-specific strategies may offer additional value for finance-related tasks.

## 2 Paper Extraction Process

To study how NLP has been applied to finance, we selected papers from 38 NLP venues, including CoLM, ACL, NAACL, EMNLP, LREC, COLING, and workshops like FinNLP and the Workshop on Economics and Natural Language Processing. The full list of venues is provided in Table [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5 "Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). As illustrated in Figure [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), we began by filtering papers that mentioned “finance” or “financial” in their abstracts. Out of all such papers published from 1975 to the present, more than 94% were published from 2017 onward. This growth coincides with the emergence of transformer-based models ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib103)), which greatly expanded the scope of NLP applications. Accordingly, we use 2017 as a threshold year for our analysis.

| Category | Description | | --- | --- | | Financial Forecast (Category I) | Targets predicting financial events, including stock movements, volatility, bankruptcy, and currency exchange rates. | | Financial Resources (Category II) | Covers tasks addressing finance-specific issues beyond prediction, such as constructing financial datasets, detecting fraud in finance-related documents, and extracting financial events. | | Financial Applications (Category III) | Focuses on general ML/NLP tasks like sentiment analysis and information/relation extraction for financial datasets. | | Finance Related (Category IV) | Covers tasks not applied to financial data or targeting financial problems, but potentially useful in finance, such privacy-preserving and explainable AI. |

This initial filtering returned 374 papers. Among them, 88 were tied to shared tasks (e.g., SemEval-2017 ([Kar et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib48)), FinCausal-2022 ([Mondal et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib76))), and 65 used the term “financial” in a different contexts – such as referencing financial resources ([Sekeres et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib90); [Ding & Riloff 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib23)) – without any actual financial application. After removing these, we retained 221 papers for our analysis.

Unlike previous surveys, which often emphasize qualitative observations, our study combines both qualitative and quantitative methods to provide a broader view of the field. We categorized the selected papers by their primary focus, resulting in four task-based categories (Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). This classification helps us examine trends in how NLP techniques are being used to tackle finance-relevant problems and supports more detailed comparisons across types of tasks.

## 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications

To understand how NLP has been used in financial contexts, we categorized papers into four groups (shown in Table [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2 Paper Extraction Process ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) based on their primary tasks (Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). This classification helps map how language modeling techniques are applied and how directly each paper engages with finance, with Category I representing the most direct financial use cases. Detailed descriptions of each category are provided in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A4 "Appendix D Task Description ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities").

Financial Forecast (Category I) papers cover predictive tasks such as stock price and volatility forecasting. While these areas are well-studied, others like economic forecasting ([Arno et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib8)), risk assessment ([Zhou et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib124)), and cryptocurrency prediction ([Seroyizhko et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib91)) receive less focus. These areas present opportunities for expanding the reach of prediction models and improving their robustness and comparability (Section [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7 "7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

Financial Resources (Category II) papers often focus on dataset construction (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). These datasets – ranging from annotated earnings calls to news and speeches – support tasks like financial event extraction ([Huang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib38); [Ju et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib47)), fraud detection ([Erben & Waldis 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib28); [Wang et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib105)), and annotation ([Aguda et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib4); [Khatuya et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib50)). Although these tasks contribute to enhancing financial data processing, other tasks remain relatively underrepresented.

In the Financial Applications (Category III) group, sentiment analysis ([Rodriguez Inserte et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib83)), information extraction ([Lior et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib60)), and question answering ([Kosireddy et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib53)) are the dominant tasks. These methods are widely used to analyze earnings calls, reports, and market commentary, where investor sentiment and factual extraction are key inputs for decision-making. Recent efforts have aimed to improve QA models for handling financial text ([Theuma & Shareghi 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib98); [Liu et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib63); [Mavi et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib72)).

Finally, among Finance-Related (Category IV) papers, the most studied areas are dataset construction and numerical reasoning. While these datasets are not finance-specific, they have potential applications in finance. For instance, fake news detection datasets ([Vargas et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib102)) can help reduce misinformation in markets. Numerical reasoning ([Akhtar et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib6)), important for understanding financial statements and assessing risk, is receiving more attention. However, other areas – such as explainable AI (XAI) ([Klein & Walther 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib52)) and privacy-preserving methods ([Abbe et al. 2012](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib1)) – remain rarely explored, despite their relevance to secure and interpretable decision-making ([Basu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib10)).

chunks.text: ## 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets

heading_path: Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities
chunks.text:
#### Acceleration of Model Adoption

Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Language Models) shows how quickly language models are adopted for finance-related NLP tasks. While early models like BERT ([Devlin et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib22)) took 13 months to appear in these applications, recent models – GPT-3.5, GPT-4 ([Achiam et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib2)), and Mistral ([Jiang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib45)) – were adopted within 6–12 months. LLaMA-2 ([Touvron et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib99))) saw integration in just 5 months, reflecting the community’s increasing speed in applying general NLP advances to financial tasks.

heading_path: Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities
chunks.text:
#### Dominance of General-Purpose Models

As shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") (Language Models), general-purpose models – LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, and Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) like BERT and RoBERTa ([Liu et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib65))) – are used far more frequently than domain-adapted ones. BERT appears in over 70 papers, while finance-tuned models such as FinBERT ([Araci 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib7); [Yang et al. 2020b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib116); [Liu et al. 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib66); [Huang et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib36)), FinMA ([Xie et al. 2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib110)), and FinGPT ([Yang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib114)) are less common. Notably, earlier FinBERT versions are more widely used than later ones, suggesting that improvements in general models often outweigh the benefits of domain-specific adaptation.

heading_path: Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities
chunks.text:
#### Decline of Custom Architectures

Custom models were common before 2022, especially for tasks like table-based QA (e.g., TagOp for TAT-QA ([Zhu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib125)), HyBrider for HybridQA ([Chen et al. 2020c](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib18))). Some models, like MDRM ([Qin & Yang 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib82)), HTML ([Yang et al. 2020a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib115)), and HAN ([Hu et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib35)), are still used as baselines, particularly in volatility prediction ([Niu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib79); [Mathur et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib71)). However, the rise of general LLMs has led to a sharp decline in custom architectures. As a result of the accelerated development and deployment of these general purpose models, researchers increasingly rely on adapting pretrained models instead of building domain-specific ones from scratch.

heading_path: Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities
chunks.text:
#### Language Coverage in Datasets

The OL and FD sections of Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") highlights the scarcity of non-English datasets for forecasting tasks such as return or volatility prediction. One exception is CMIN ([Luo et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib67)), which includes English and Chinese financial data. Most datasets use English-only sources like EDGAR filings ([Maheshwari et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib69)) and financial news ([Xie et al. 2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib111)), which may limit model performance in non-English markets. Creating multilingual forecasting datasets would support broader applicability and reduce language bias, as also noted by [Jørgensen et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib46).

Since 2017, research applying NLP to finance has shifted from custom models toward general-purpose pretrained architectures. New models are adopted faster than before, and general PLMs have largely replaced finance-specific ones. This preference also influences dataset use: most forecasting datasets are English-only, limiting generalization to global markets.

## 5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance

To understand the methodological landscape, we grouped the approaches used in the surveyed papers into nine categories (Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A3 "Appendix C Common Methods used ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Common Methods used ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While the total number of papers has grown, methods like statistical NLP, conventional machine learning, and embeddings have remained mostly flat. In contrast, there has been a sharp increase in the use of deep learning, PLMs and LLMs, reflecting the field’s shift toward pretrained architectures.

#### Shift Toward PLMs and LLMs

As seen in Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), the first three categories – statistical NLP, embeddings, and conventional ML – have persisted but have seen reduced usage as PLMs and LLMs take lead. The rise began with models like BERT in 2019, which significantly improved context handling in financial texts ([Li et al. 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib55); [Chen et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib17); [Ein-Dor et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib27)). PLMs are now widely used for tasks such as summarization and entity recognition. Since 2023, LLMs like ChatGPT-3.5 have seen rapid adoption ([Tang et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib97); [Li et al. 2023a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib56); [Ni et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib77)), especially for text generation ([Guo et al. 2023b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib34)) and financial QA ([Uluoglakci & Temizel 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib100)). This transition has also brought more complex deep learning architectures used for multi-step reasoning and domain-specific challenges ([Ma et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib68); [Zhao et al. 2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib120); [Su et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib95)).

#### Underexplored Techniques

While pretrained models dominate, several methods remain underused despite their promise. Statistical modeling, graph-based approaches, and knowledge graphs could improve model robustness and interpretability, particularly for applications like causality detection ([Tabari et al. 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib96)) or market dynamics ([Menzio et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib73)). Emerging techniques like GraphRAG ([Edge et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib26)) highlight the potential of such methods, yet they appear in only a fraction of papers. Their limited presence suggests opportunities for expanding methodological diversity in future research.

## 6 Code & Data Accessibility

As the adoption of language models accelerates, the issue of open accessibility in NLP research, especially in finance, becomes more relevant. As shown in Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6 Code & Data Accessibility ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), open-source practices have become more common in recent years. Before 2021, closed-source code dominated, but the trend has shifted toward sharing code and datasets. This move enhances transparency, reproducibility, and collaborative progress in NLP research applied to finance ([Whited 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib106)). Despite this, some papers still include inactive links or empty repositories, limiting reproducibility. At the same time, dataset availability has steadily increased since 2017, pointing to growing awareness around open data. Maintaining functional, up-to-date repositories remains essential to support meaningful benchmarking and model development.

## 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting

Category I papers reveal several areas where forecasting models could be improved. Most studies use general ML metrics, leaving out finance-specific measures that better capture practical utility. Crisis periods are rarely considered, limiting insights into how models behave under stress. Finally, there is a strong U.S. and English-language bias in data, with limited adoption of global financial datasets. Expanding these areas of exploration could strengthen model robustness and support broader real-world applicability.

chunks.text:
### 7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics

As shown in Figure [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), Category I papers mostly rely on ML metrics like accuracy, F1, or MSE ([Sawhney et al. 2020b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib87); [Wu 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib107); [Yangjia et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib117)). While useful, these do not fully reflect financial performance. Only three financial metrics appear more than once – Sharpe Ratio, Maximum Drawdown, and Cumulative Return (defined in Appendix [G](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A7 "Appendix G Glossary ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

Finance-specific metrics offer risk-adjusted insights that ML measures overlook. Sharpe Ratio, for example, evaluates return relative to risk ([Zou et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib127)). Incorporating such metrics would improve comparability across models and align research outcomes with practical needs ([Zhang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib118); [Zou et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib127); [Sawhney et al. 2021b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib89)).

### 7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing

Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") shows that data usage begins to rise after 1993, when electronic filings became publicly available, with another increase in 2005 following the HTML filing mandate ([U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib101)). However, usage dips around 2009 and 2020 – years associated with the global financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic. These periods are essential for evaluating model robustness, yet they remain underused, likely due to data availability challenges prior to 2015 ([Bloomberg L.P. 2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib11)).

Despite these constraints, crisis periods offer valuable testing grounds. Most models are trained on stable conditions, which may not reflect their behavior during volatility. Including data from crises enables stress testing ([Investopedia Staff 2025b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib42)) and helps build forecasting models that remain reliable under instability.

#### Commonly Used and Overlooked Data Sources

Most forecasting models use common financial sources: stock prices, SEC filings, financial news, earnings calls (e.g., MDRM ([Qin & Yang 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib82)), StockNet ([Xu & Cohen 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib113))). But many valuable datasets are either rarely used (e.g., Federal Reserve reports ([Menzio et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib73))) or completely absent from NLP research. Public resources like FRED ([Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib30)) and Fama-French ([Fama & French 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#bib.bib29)) offer rich macroeconomic indicators that remain unexplored. Incorporating these datasets could help capture macroeconomic trends and market dynamics, improving model reliability.

chunks.text:
#### Data Accessibility and Maintenance

Access limitations are also a concern. Legacy datasets like MDRM are outdated, and APIs such as Yahoo Finance’s have been discontinued. Others, like CRSP, require paid access. This limits reproducibility and restricts access to reliable, up-to-date data. There’s a clear need for open, regularly updated datasets applicable for financial forecasting.

## 8 Discussion & Conclusion

This paper presents a systematic, quantitative analysis of NLP research applied to finance. From an initial pool of 374 papers across major NLP venues (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A5 "Appendix E Conference Proceedings ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")), we curated a final set of 221 papers after filtering. We categorized them by primary task (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and assessed each across 11 qualitative and quantitative dimensions (Table [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix B Various Dimensions surveyed ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S8.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 8 Discussion & Conclusion ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities") summarizes key trends and identifies opportunities where language modeling research can further contribute to finance-related problems.

Forecasting is mostly centered around stock and volatility prediction. | Underexplored areas such as explainability, privacy-preserving methods, and tasks like bankruptcy or cryptocurrency prediction present valuable directions for future work (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). | | PLM/LLM Adoption | General-purpose PLMs and LLMs have largely replaced finance-specific and custom architectures. #### Implications for NLP & LM Researchers

NLP research applied to finance has largely centered on a few core tasks – sentiment analysis, information extraction, and question answering – while underexploring others like explainability and privacy-preserving methods (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S3 "3 Task Distribution in NLP for Financial Applications ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). The rapid adoption of PLMs and LLMs has made it easier to apply language models, but has also led to reduced methodological variety (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S4 "4 Language Model Adoption & Datasets ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Graph-based models, statistical techniques, and other alternatives remain underused despite their potential (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S5 "5 Methods Used in NLP for Finance ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). While open-source practices have become more common, researchers should be more careful about maintaining functional and up-to-date repositories to ensure long-term reproducibility and meaningful benchmarking (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6 Code & Data Accessibility ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). In addition, adopting financial-domain metrics can make evaluations more meaningful and aligned with practical goals (Section [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Including crisis periods in datasets (Section [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) and improving data selection practices (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")) can help ensure robustness and consistency. More diverse datasets, especially beyond English and U.S. markets, are also needed to broaden applicability (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")).

chunks.text:
#### Considerations for Financial Practitioners

While NLP methods are increasingly used in financial contexts, several challenges remain. Many models are trained on static or incomplete datasets, leading to biases that may affect predictions (Section [7.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS3 "7.3 Data Sources ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Evaluations often omit real-world considerations such as market volatility and financial risk (Sections [7.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS2 "7.2 Crisis Years for Stress Testing ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities"), [7.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2504.07274#S7.SS1 "7.1 Potential in Financial Metrics ‣ 7 Potential in Financial Forecasting ‣ Language Modeling for the Future of Finance: A Quantitative Survey into Metrics, Tasks, and Data Opportunities")). Incorporating financial benchmarks and testing models under stress conditions could improve their practical value. Continued progress in this direction can better align research outcomes with decision-making needs in financial settings.

## Ethics Statement

This study does not assess the merit or quality of individual papers. We do not suggest that any category or method is inherently better than others. Our goal is to map the volume and distribution of research applying NLP methods to finance, and to offer a foundation for further study, without making judgments about the value of specific approaches.
